body.text: On November 19, the Rohingya community will finally hear the decision of the judges at the International Court of Justice (ICJ). The court will decide whether the atrocities they suffered at the hands of the Myanmar military meet one of the most demanding legal thresholds in international law that are required to establish genocide.

It took nine years to get here: nine years of giving statements to investigators, speaking to lawyers, and reliving killings, rapes, gang rapes, tortures, displacements, and other losses. Throughout interviews that demanded immense courage, Rohingya survivors have tirelessly helped document what their community has lived through. They have watched, indefatigably, as people who were not there when crimes took place, weighed which word should be used to describe the targeted, deliberate violence unleashed on them, their families and their community in an attempt to erase them. Yet through it all, they maintained an astonishing capacity to hope and an unwavering determination to get justice.

In a few days, Rohingya survivors, supported by Legal Action Worldwide (LAW), which represents them in these proceedings, will enter, one last time, the Great Hall of Justice in The Hague. They will seek justice for witness NJ’s daughter, a newborn ripped from her mother’s arms, stabbed to death, and thrown into a fire. They will seek justice for witness MN’s father, an eight-year-old nephew, and 85 other men who were massacred in Maung Nu, and whose bodies were piled on top of one another. They will seek justice for witness MS’ daughter, who was shot in the back while fleeing the attack on her village. They will seek justice for the tens of thousands of Rohingya who were intentionally executed, burned, raped and gang raped, tortured, drowned, stabbed, beheaded, and mutilated, and the million others who have lived in exile ever since.

In court, a few meters away, will be Myanmar military’s agents, representing those who planned, coordinated and executed the genocidal “clearance operations” in 2017, and have denied responsibility ever since, despite the overwhelming evidence to the contrary presented to the ICJ. The United Nations, international organizations such as LAW, and independent experts have all reached the same conclusion: That the Myanmar military knew exactly what it was doing. It acted meticulously, in an organized and systematic manner, driven by hatred towards the Rohingya and the willingness to kill children, women, men, and elders.

The proceedings were equally unprecedented in scale. In addition to The Gambia, which initiated the case, 11 states have intervened to address the interpretation of the Genocide Convention in favor of the Rohingya. The judges examined survivor testimony, expert analysis, satellite imagery, U.N. documentation, and extensive legal arguments. The Gambia argued that the scale and pattern of Myanmar’s conduct demonstrated genocidal intent. Myanmar has insisted that its military operations were legitimate responses to terrorism.
The judges will now decide how international law characterizes what happened.

They may conclude that Myanmar bears direct responsibility for genocide against the Rohingya. They may find a narrower breach of the Genocide Convention: that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide, failed to punish it, enabled it through complicity or incitement, failed to enact the necessary laws, or violated the Court’s earlier orders to protect the Rohingya while the case was pending. They may produce a divided judgment that leaves some central questions unresolved. They may even decide – though it is hard to imagine – that the evidentiary threshold required under international law has not been met to find that a genocide took place.

Each outcome carries different legal consequences, different opportunities for accountability, and different implications for survivors. But none would erase what happened, nor change the fact that Rohingya families were driven from their homes, that entire villages were destroyed, that women and girls suffered horrific sexual violence, and that survivors have spent years fighting to have their experiences recognized and acknowledged.

States will have immediate responsibilities. They should review the arms transfers, aviation fuel supplies, banking links and economic relationships that sustain Myanmar’s military. They must support a register documenting Rohingya losses and a properly funded reparations mechanism, such as a trust fund, that could be constituted with Myanmar’s official frozen assets. They must protect refugees against forced or premature return and sustain humanitarian support in Bangladesh.

Given the regional migration routes and the number of people risking their lives to seek refuge, ASEAN countries must adopt a coordinated, rights-based approach to people fleeing Myanmar by providing individual protection screening and temporary legal status. Moreover, they must uphold the absolute prohibition on forced return to danger. Community-based alternatives for inclusion could replace immigration detention, including through access to work, healthcare and education, and the establishment of safe legal pathways and predictable arrangements for rescue and disembarkation at sea

When the judges speak next week, they will mark the beginning of the next phase of the Rohingya’s pursuit of justice – and of international justice itself. A finding of genocide would create the strongest foundation for reparations, accountability measures, citizenship rights, and safe returns. A more limited finding would still carry serious legal and political weight. Even a disappointing outcome would, hopefully, encourage governments to pursue accountability via other avenues, including the International Criminal Court, universal jurisdiction proceedings, and national courts.

Courtroom intervention must now become action outside the courtroom. When the judges enter the Great Hall, they will speak in the language of law. They must. Genocide cases depend on evidence, intent, attribution and strict legal standards. But behind every paragraph and every word, they place at the center the reality of the people who lived through and died from these atrocities.

One survivor told me she would testify ten more times if needed. That sentence still haunts me, and it should shame all of us. Because no survivor should have to repeat, again and again, that their child was murdered, their village burned, their body violated and their people targeted.
The Rohingya have told the truth. Now the Court will speak. And when it does, the world must act.
